0.title: Strength and Dignity in Christ
0.essay:
What does it mean to be a woman? Our culture gives many answers, and most of them are exhausting. The Bible offers something far better.

Exhausting answers

Some say a woman’s worth lies in her beauty, her body and her appeal to others. Some say it lies in her career and independence, and that marriage or motherhood will hold her back. Others say womanhood is simply whatever an individual chooses it to be. And sadly, some religious cultures have reduced women to silence and household duties alone, ignoring the many women Scripture honours for their wisdom, courage, faith and work.

Defined by God

A woman is not defined by her looks, her relationships, her achievements or anyone’s opinion. She is defined by the God who made her. “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). A woman is fully an image-bearer of God, equal in dignity with man, loved by God and called by him.

Women who lived it

The Bible shows us women who lived that calling. Sarah, who hoped in God. Ruth, whose loyal love brought her into the family line of Christ. Hannah, who poured out her heart in prayer. Abigail, whose wisdom stopped a massacre. Mary, who said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). The women who stayed at the cross when most of the disciples had fled, and who were the first to hear that Jesus had risen. Priscilla, Phoebe, Lydia, Lois and Eunice. Scripture’s picture of womanhood is rich, strong and beautiful.

Proverbs gives a summary worth carrying through these studies: “Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come” (Proverbs 31:25). Biblical womanhood is a woman’s glad embrace of God’s design: clothed in strength and dignity, fearing the LORD, and using her gifts to help, nurture and build up others for the glory of Christ.

Where these studies stand

These studies follow the historic Reformed understanding usually called complementarian: men and women are equal in worth, but God has given them distinct and complementary callings, especially in marriage and in the leadership of the church. Many sincere Christians, usually called egalitarians, read some key passages differently, and where those questions arise their view is explained fairly.

These studies are for every woman: single or married, with children or without, young or old. A woman’s calling is not on hold until she marries, and her worth does not depend on whether she becomes a mother.

Grace first

Above all, womanhood, like manhood, is not a standard to earn God’s love. It flows from grace. Every woman who belongs to Christ is part of the bride he loved and gave himself for, and he will present her “in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

The chapters

Made in God’s Image: A Helper Fit for Him; Eve, the Fall and the Promised Offspring; Jesus and the Women Who Followed Him; Wives: Strength Under Christ; Women in the Church; and Beauty That Lasts.

For reflection

What messages about womanhood have shaped you most, from family, church or culture? Which of them fit the Bible?

1.title: Made in God's Image: A Helper Fit for Him
1.essay:
Womanhood begins in the heart of God. A woman does not borrow her dignity from a man. She receives it directly from her Creator.

Image-bearer from the beginning

The first description of humanity in the Bible includes women from the very start: “male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The woman is not an afterthought or a lesser copy of the man. She bears the image of God fully. Both man and woman were blessed. Both were given dominion over the earth. Both were called very good.

To bear God’s image is to reflect his character and represent his rule in the world. Every woman, whatever her age, ability, marital status or background, carries that dignity. This is the foundation of everything else Scripture says about women.

Not good to be alone

Genesis 2 tells the story in more detail. God formed the man and placed him in the garden. Then, for the first time in creation, he said something was not good: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18). The ESV notes that “fit for” may be translated “corresponding to.” The woman would be like the man and yet different from him, his counterpart, the one who completes the picture.

The woman was not created because the man was superior, but because he was lacking. She brought what he needed. In marriage, a wife is her husband’s partner in life and in God’s calling, his closest ally. And even for a woman who is not married, the verse reminds us that God made human beings for relationship, and that women have a vital part in building up others.

Built with care

God then made the woman in a remarkable way. “And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man” (Genesis 2:22). The ESV notes that the Hebrew says God “built” her. She was not formed from dust like the man, but carefully built, as an architect crafts a masterpiece.

When Adam saw her, he said, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man” (Genesis 2:23). In Hebrew the words for woman and man sound alike. She shared his very nature.

Many women today measure themselves constantly against images of beauty, success and motherhood on their screens, and always come up short. Genesis speaks a better word. Your worth was settled when God made you in his image and built you with care. It is not measured by likes, weight, income or anyone’s approval.

Helper as honour

Some people hear the word helper and think of a servant or an assistant. But the Bible uses the same word of God himself. David, hunted by enemies, said, “Behold, God is my helper” (Psalm 54:4). Another psalm says, “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:2). God is not a helper because he is weaker than David. He is a helper because he brings the strength David lacks.

That transforms how we read Genesis 2:18. To help is not to be inferior. It is to bring strength that another person needs. To help is to be like God. And the woman’s calling as helper is part of God’s good design before the fall, not a punishment after it.

Some women hear “helper” and assume they must suppress their gifts, opinions and strength. But the God who is our helper is never weak or silent. A wife who helps her husband brings her whole self: her insight, her counsel, her courage and her faith. Abigail’s wisdom, later in Scripture, shows how valuable a woman’s discernment can be.

Equal heirs

Women and men are equally made in God’s image, equally fallen and equally redeemed. Peter calls wives “heirs with you of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7). He calls the wife “the weaker vessel,” most likely referring to physical strength, not her mind, spirit or worth. And the very reason he gives for honouring her is that she is an equal heir of eternal life. He adds a warning: a husband who dishonours his wife will find his prayers hindered. God takes the dignity of women so seriously that how a man treats his wife affects his relationship with God.

Paul says that “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). No woman is a second-class Christian.

Different and complementary

Yet God did not make two identical people. He made a man and a woman who correspond to each other. Their differences are not flaws to be erased but gifts that let them serve together in ways neither could alone. “Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman” (1 Corinthians 11:11). A godly woman uses her gifts, wisdom and strength to strengthen others: in marriage for those who are married, and in her family, church and world.

For reflection

How does it change your view of the word “helper” to know that God calls himself his people’s helper? Where are you tempted to find your worth in comparison with other women, and what truth from Genesis speaks to that?

2.title: Eve, the Fall and the Promised Offspring
2.essay:
The goodness of creation did not last. Yet in the same chapter that records the woman’s sin, God makes a promise that centres on a woman and her child.

The lie in the garden

The serpent came to the woman and questioned God’s word and his goodness. Eve listened, and “when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate” (Genesis 3:6).

Her sin followed a pattern that is still familiar. What God had forbidden began to look desirable, beautiful and wise. Temptation always works this way: it makes disobedience look good. And her sin did not stay with her. Our sins always affect those closest to us, just as our faithfulness can bless them.

The same lie comes to women today: God’s design is restrictive, his commands keep you from happiness, you can be wise without him. Every generation of women, and of men, must decide whom to believe.

Deceived but not discarded

The New Testament says that “the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning” (2 Corinthians 11:3). She was deceived, and Adam, standing beside her, sinned knowingly. Both were guilty. Both hid. Both received consequences. But Scripture never treats women as more sinful than men. “Sin came into the world through one man” (Romans 5:12). And God pursued Eve with grace, clothing her and Adam, and promising a Saviour through her offspring.

Pain where joy was meant to be

For the woman, the consequences touched the two areas of life meant to bring the greatest joy: childbearing and marriage. “I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16).

The ESV notes that “for” may be read “against,” and points to Genesis 4:7, where sin’s desire is against Cain. Many understand Genesis 3:16 to describe a struggle that sin brought into marriage: the wife tempted to resist or control her husband, the husband tempted to dominate her harshly. This is the curse, not God’s design. It describes what sin does; it is not a command to follow. Christian marriage, shaped by the gospel, is meant to undo it, as husbands love sacrificially and wives respond with trust and respect.

Many women know Genesis 3:16 first-hand: the pain of childbirth, miscarriage, infertility, or the heartbreak of raising children in a fallen world. Genesis does not hide that pain. But it sets it beside a promise.

The first gospel

Before God spoke to the woman, he spoke to the serpent: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). This is often called the first announcement of the gospel.

Eve had listened to the serpent as a friend. God would make them enemies again. And a descendant of the woman would strike the decisive blow: the serpent would only bruise his heel, but he would crush the serpent’s head. That was fulfilled at the cross, where Jesus was wounded and yet defeated Satan. The first gospel promise in the Bible centres on a woman and her child.

Mother of all living

In spite of her sin, Eve was not abandoned. Adam named her Eve, “because she was the mother of all living” (Genesis 3:20). The word offspring is literally “seed,” and the promise follows that seed through the whole Bible, through the births of children to women like Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and finally Mary. God used women again and again to carry forward his plan of salvation.

Then Paul sums it all up: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman” (Galatians 4:4). The eternal Son of God entered the world the way every human being does, through a mother’s body. God honoured womanhood by choosing it as the doorway through which the Saviour would come. The woman through whom sin entered the world became the ancestor of the child who would destroy it.

A hard verse

Paul writes that “she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control” (1 Timothy 2:15). Christians have understood this in several ways: that women are saved through the birth of the Child, Christ; that women are kept safe through the dangers of childbirth; or that women work out their salvation in faithfully living their God-given calling, including motherhood. Whatever the exact sense, Paul is not teaching that women earn salvation by having babies. Salvation is by grace through faith, for women and men alike.

Hope in the pain

Every Christian mother raising children in hope, and every woman grieving the children she longed for, can look to the Child who was born to crush the serpent and who will one day wipe away every tear.

For reflection

In what ways are women today tempted to doubt that God’s design is good? How might the words “born of woman” encourage a woman who struggles to see her life as significant?

3.title: Jesus and the Women Who Followed Him
3.essay:
In the first-century world, women were often overlooked. Many teachers would not teach them, and their testimony was often discounted. Jesus broke with all of that.

The woman at the well

Even Jesus’ disciples “marveled that he was talking with a woman” (John 4:27). He spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well, a woman with a broken past whom others avoided, and revealed himself to her as the Messiah. She had been married five times and was living with a man who was not her husband. Yet she became one of the first evangelists in the Gospels. She went back to the town that probably looked down on her and invited them to come and see. “Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony” (John 4:39). God delights to use unlikely people, including women with painful pasts, to point others to Christ.

Forgiven and restored

Jesus allowed a sinful woman to wash his feet with her tears, and declared, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). Mary Magdalene had been set free from seven demons (Luke 8:2). Many of the women who met Jesus came with painful pasts. He did not define them by it. He forgave, healed and restored them. No woman is beyond his grace.

Disciples, not spectators

Mary of Bethany sat at the Lord’s feet, the place a student took before a teacher. Martha, busy serving, was frustrated that her sister was not helping. Jesus did not condemn Martha’s service, but he gently corrected her anxious heart: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42). And he defended Mary: “Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

Women are not only called to serve Christ with their hands. They are invited to sit at his feet, learn his word and know him deeply. Martha too grew in understanding. At her brother’s death she made one of the great confessions of the Gospels: “I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world” (John 11:27).

Remembered

When a woman anointed Jesus with costly ointment and others scolded her, he praised her and said, “wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her” (Mark 14:9).

Supporting the mission

Luke gives a surprising picture of Jesus’ travelling ministry. Along with the twelve were some women who had been healed: Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager, Susanna, “and many others, who provided for them out of their means” (Luke 8:3). Their discipleship grew out of gratitude. They used their money and resources to support the spread of the gospel. Grace brought very different women together, from the royal court to the margins, in the service of Christ.

Today many churches and missions are sustained by the generosity, prayers and practical care of women who rarely receive attention. Jesus notices, and Scripture records their names.

At the cross

When the soldiers came, the disciples ran. But at the cross, “There were also women looking on from a distance” (Mark 15:40): Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome and many others. They could not stop the crucifixion, but they would not abandon their Lord. Faithfulness in the dark hours, simply staying when others leave, is one of the great strengths the Gospels show in women.

The first witnesses

On Easter morning, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb weeping, and the risen Jesus called her by name. Then he sent her with a message to the disciples. She became the first to announce, “I have seen the Lord” (John 20:18). Other women, too, were sent from the empty tomb to tell the disciples (Matthew 28:5–8).

The central claim of Christianity, that Jesus is alive, was first spoken by a woman. In a culture that discounted women’s testimony, God gave women the privilege of announcing the heart of the faith. Every Christian woman who tells others about Jesus is following in Mary’s footsteps.

The twelve

Jesus did not erase the differences between men and women. He chose twelve men as apostles. Complementarians see this as consistent with the later New Testament pattern of male elders. Egalitarians often see it as a concession to the culture of the time. Either way, Jesus’ treatment of women shows that no restriction on church office can ever mean that women are less valued or less gifted.

He taught women, forgave them, healed them, received their gifts and entrusted them with the greatest news in history. Every woman who follows Christ today follows a Lord who sees her, values her and calls her to serve him.

For reflection

Which of the women Jesus met do you relate to most, and why? Where does your life need more of Mary, and where more of Martha? How could you use your resources, like the women of Luke 8, to support the work of the gospel?

4.title: Wives: Strength Under Christ
4.essay:
“Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). To many modern ears this sounds like weakness, inferiority or even abuse. Read carefully, it says something very different.

Four things to notice

First, it is addressed to wives, not to women in general. Paul says “your own husbands.” Women are not called to submit to all men.

Second, it is voluntary. Paul speaks to the wife herself, not to the husband. Nowhere does the Bible tell husbands to make their wives submit.

Third, it is “as to the Lord.” A wife’s submission is ultimately an act of trust in Christ, not in her husband’s perfection. Her husband may be imperfect, but her obedience is directed to the perfect Lord.

Fourth, it has limits. No wife is called to follow her husband into sin, for “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). And no wife is called to submit to abuse, to cover up crime or to disobey God.

The headship of a Saviour

Paul explains the pattern: the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, and he immediately adds that Christ is its Saviour (Ephesians 5:23). The headship Paul describes is that of a Saviour who dies for his bride. And Paul then spends far more words calling husbands to that kind of love (Ephesians 5:25–33). A wife is not called to submit to a tyrant, but to trust a husband who is himself commanded to love her like Christ.

Paul grounds all this in a greater reality: “Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands” (Ephesians 5:24). Christian marriage is a living picture of the gospel. The husband’s sacrificial love pictures Christ’s love, and the wife’s glad trust and respect picture the church’s response.

Submission is not inferiority

“The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3), and the Son willingly submits to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:28), though he is fully equal to him. Submission within an order of roles says nothing about lesser worth. A wife who submits to her husband is doing something Christ himself does.

Submission is not silence

Submission means that a wife honours her husband’s God-given responsibility to lead, supports him, respects him (Ephesians 5:33) and seeks to help him lead well. It does not mean silence. A wise wife speaks, advises, disagrees when necessary and brings all her gifts to the marriage.

The woman of Proverbs 31 is an acrostic portrait, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: an A to Z of a wise, godly woman, not a checklist every woman must complete. “An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels” (Proverbs 31:10). “The heart of her husband trusts in her” (Proverbs 31:11). “She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life” (Proverbs 31:12). She buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business, cares for the poor and speaks with wisdom. “She dresses herself with strength” (Proverbs 31:17), literally “she girds her loins,” a picture of preparing for hard work. Biblical womanhood is not passive. It is strong.

Abigail

Abigail was married to Nabal, a man described as “harsh and badly behaved” (1 Samuel 25:3). When his foolishness put the whole household in danger, she acted quickly, met David and persuaded him not to take revenge. David said, “Blessed be your discretion” (1 Samuel 25:33). Her story shows that godly womanhood includes courage, initiative and wisdom, especially when a husband is failing.

Won without a word

Peter writes to wives married to unbelievers. In a world where wives were expected to follow their husbands’ religion, these women had chosen Christ. Peter does not tell them to leave or to argue their husbands into faith. He tells them to live so that “even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1).

Many Christian women are married to men who do not share their faith, or whose faith has grown cold. This does not forbid speaking about Christ. It means that constant pressure and nagging rarely win hearts, while a life of respect, purity and peace speaks powerfully over time. A wife’s godly life can be the most powerful sermon her husband ever hears.

The beauty of the heart

Peter goes on: “let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious” (1 Peter 3:4). He is not forbidding women to care about their appearance. He is saying where true beauty lies. Outward beauty fades, and our culture’s obsession with it leaves many women anxious and insecure. This beauty grows with age.

A gentle and quiet spirit is not a matter of personality. Outgoing, energetic women can have it. It is a heart at rest in God, not anxious, controlling or fearful. Peter adds that such women “do not fear anything that is frightening” (1 Peter 3:6).

The two views

Christians differ on these passages. Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, see a real and loving pattern of headship and submission in marriage, rooted in creation and modelled on Christ and the church. Egalitarians often stress Ephesians 5:21, “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ,” and see the specific instructions to wives as applying Christian humility within first-century household customs. Both agree that husbands and wives are equal before God, that the husband must love sacrificially, and that no one may use these verses to oppress.

For reflection

What misunderstandings of “submission” have you heard, and how does Ephesians 5 correct them? What does “a gentle and quiet spirit” look like in a woman with a strong, outgoing personality?

5.title: Women in the Church: Gifts, Ministry and Order
5.essay:
The New Testament church was full of women serving Christ. The church is always poorer when their gifts are neglected.

Women at work in the early church

Women prayed and prophesied in the gatherings (1 Corinthians 11:5; Acts 21:9), just as Joel had promised: “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17). Older women taught and trained younger women (Titus 2:3–5). Lydia opened her home to Paul and to the believers in Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40). Euodia and Syntyche laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel (Philippians 4:3).

When the eloquent preacher Apollos was found to have an incomplete understanding, Priscilla and Aquila “took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). Priscilla’s name often comes first in the New Testament, which may suggest she was especially prominent. Her knowledge of Scripture strengthened the church.

Phoebe is the first person Paul greets in Romans: “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae” (Romans 16:1). The ESV notes that “servant” may be translated “deaconess.” She was also “a patron of many and of myself as well” (Romans 16:2). Many believe she carried this very letter to Rome. The most important letter Paul ever wrote may have been placed in a woman’s hands to deliver, and perhaps to explain.

Every believer gifted

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10). The Holy Spirit gives gifts to women as freely as to men, and the church needs every one of them.

Let a woman learn

At the same time, Paul writes, “Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve” (1 Timothy 2:11–13).

Notice how the passage begins: “Let a woman learn.” In a culture where women were often denied religious education, that was a remarkable command. Christian women are to study God’s word deeply and gladly.

How do these fit together?

Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, understand Paul to be reserving the office of elder or pastor, and the authoritative teaching of the whole church that belongs to it, to qualified men. They note that Paul grounds this in creation, not culture. They see Priscilla’s private teaching of Apollos as fully consistent with this, since it was not the public teaching office of the church.

Egalitarians read the same passages differently. Many believe Paul was addressing a specific problem in Ephesus, such as false teachers influencing untaught women. They point to Deborah the judge (Judges 4:4), to Phoebe, and to Junia, whom Paul describes as “well known to the apostles” (Romans 16:7), as evidence that women may hold any office. Complementarians reply that the ESV notes Junia may be read “Junias,” and “apostles” may mean messengers rather than the Twelve.

The Reformed tradition has differed on whether women may serve as deacons, but has generally held that the elder’s office is for men. Faithful Christians who love Scripture hold both views, and the question should be discussed with humility and charity.

More than the kitchen and the nursery

Women may and should use their gifts in countless ways: teaching women and children, prophesying, evangelising, counselling, leading ministries, serving as deacons in many churches, showing hospitality and mercy, and much more.

Some churches have limited women’s service to cooking, cleaning and childcare. Those are valuable ministries, and Jesus honours them. But the New Testament shows women teaching, evangelising, supporting missions, opening their homes for churches, prophesying and labouring in the gospel. A church that holds complementarian convictions should be the first to open every door of service that Scripture leaves open.

Spiritual mothers

Paul gives older women a teaching ministry: “Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good, and so train the young women to love their husbands and children” (Titus 2:3–4). The curriculum is the whole Christian life: love, self-control, purity, managing the home, kindness. And the reason: “that the word of God may not be reviled” (Titus 2:5). When Christian women live and teach well, the gospel is honoured.

Some of the most powerful ministry in any church is done by older women who disciple younger women in faith, marriage, motherhood and daily life. Paul writes, “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well” (Romans 16:13). We know nothing else about her, except that she cared for the great apostle like a son. Many women without children of their own, or whose children are grown, become spiritual mothers to younger believers. That is ministry of the highest value.

For reflection

Make a list of the ways women served in the New Testament church. Which are encouraged in your church today? Who has been a spiritual mother to you, and whom could you encourage?

6.title: Beauty That Lasts: Singleness, Motherhood and the Fear of the LORD
6.essay:
The Proverbs 31 poem ends with the key to everything: “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30).

The fear of the LORD

Charm can be a mask. Beauty is vain, fleeting like a breath. Our culture spends enormous energy on both. But the praise goes to the woman who fears the LORD, who lives in reverent awe of him, trusting and obeying him. The whole book of Proverbs begins and ends with the fear of the LORD. The excellent woman is not praised first for her productivity or her looks, but for her trust in God. That is the root from which every other virtue grows.

Every woman can have that beauty, whatever her appearance, age or circumstances. And unlike charm and outward beauty, it grows richer with the years. That truth frees women in every season of life.

Singleness

Many women feel pressure to find their identity in marriage or motherhood. But Scripture honours women in every circumstance. Paul writes, “the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34). He is not saying married women do not care about the Lord, or that marriage is second-class. Marriage rightly brings responsibilities. But a single woman has a unique freedom to give undivided attention to the Lord. Paul saw singleness as an opportunity, not a tragedy.

Paul, himself single, said, “each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another” (1 Corinthians 7:7). A single woman is not an incomplete woman. Jesus, the most fully human person who ever lived, was single. Single women in the church are not waiting for their lives to begin, and the church should give them a full place in its family life.

Anna

Anna had every reason to be bitter. Her husband died after seven years of marriage, and she lived as a widow into her eighties. Instead, she gave herself to the temple, “worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day” (Luke 2:37). God rewarded her faithfulness by letting her see the infant Messiah, and she spoke of him to all who were waiting for redemption (Luke 2:38). A life that looks small to the world can be rich and fruitful before God.

Motherhood

Motherhood is a high calling. “Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD” (Psalm 127:3). Hannah was mocked for her childlessness and misunderstood even by the priest. She took her grief to God and poured out her soul. When God gave her Samuel, she said, “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him” (1 Samuel 1:27). Then she kept her promise: “Therefore I have lent him to the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:28).

Every Christian mother must learn that lesson. Our children are gifts from God, not possessions. We raise them for him, and release them into his hands. Samuel became one of Israel’s greatest prophets, and it began with a praying mother.

Lois and Eunice

Paul traces Timothy’s faith back two generations: “I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Timothy’s father was a Greek, and there is no sign he shared their faith. These two women taught Timothy the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). A grandmother’s prayers and a mother’s teaching shaped a pastor who led churches and received two letters of Scripture. Many women do their most lasting work at a kitchen table with an open Bible and a child beside them.

Yet motherhood in the church is wider than biology. Every mature woman can nurture faith in others, as Rufus’s mother did for Paul.

For those who long for children

Scripture speaks tenderly to women who long for children and have none. “He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children” (Psalm 113:9). Sometimes God answers that prayer with children of her own. Sometimes he gives spiritual children through her love and ministry. Either way, her worth before God is complete in Christ.

Laughing at the time to come

The capable woman of Proverbs 31 “laughs at the time to come” (Proverbs 31:25). She can face ageing, loss and the unknown future without fear, because her hope is in God.

For the Christian woman, that hope is sure. The whole church is Christ’s bride, and at the end of history the cry will go up: “Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). That is the destiny of every woman who belongs to him. All fading beauty will give way to glory.

For reflection

How is the fear of the LORD different from being charming or beautiful? Who were the “Lois and Eunice” figures in your own faith, and how might you pass faith on to the next generation?
